name: Dana Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, have a bachelor's degree and manage six recruiters inside a large company. I've done it nine years and I am about average at the management part; mornings are job adverts, work samples and a string of candidates asking whether anyone read their application. I use AI every day to plan interviews and compare dates, then read the samples myself. I like finding skill hidden by a job title; I hate sending a polished rejection to someone we never truly considered.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the family picture alongside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is an architect with a steady salary, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. My manager pay is high, we have about eight months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of similar hiring teams nearby. I can take a careful career risk, but the family's schedule still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the hiring team AI can sort duplicate applications and draft an interview calendar, but it shouldn't decide who gets a chance to speak. A clean queue does not prove we found the best person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI daily to compare opening dates and draft candidate notes, though I still read the actual work samples. I have managed six recruiters for nine years, earn well, and have eight months of expenses saved with my partner's steady architecture salary; our mortgage and two children's school costs are covered in a plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Monday I'll keep the human work-sample review for shortlisted candidates and use AI to draft only the interview timetable. In the first year of this plateau, we'll continue putting 200 a month in each child's education account if both salaries hold, and I'll ask rejected applicants what part of our process was confusing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the job and our household. I still wince when a good applicant can't get through a form that was meant to help us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who was lost in the form?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A candidate with years of repair work wrote 'service engineer' instead of our exact job title, and the search missed the application. Recruiter Jo found the work sample in the manual review, and we invited the candidate for a call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you automate more if the tool improved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd test it on the applications we already know, with consent, and look at who gets dropped. My family has savings; that isn't a reason to take chances with someone else's livelihood.

say: I'd use AI for **duplicate forms** and timetables, while keeping people on work-sample review.
I'd say a **clean queue** does not show whether we found the right candidate.
think: Our **eight-month cushion**, my high pay and my partner's steady wage make the plateau secure.
I use AI **daily** for dates and candidate notes, then read work samples myself.
do: Keep **human work-sample review** and draft only interview timetables with AI.
Put **200 monthly per child** into education accounts while both salaries hold.
feel: She feels **calm** about income and bothered by applicants lost in a tidy process.
S0.quote: My family has savings; that isn't a reason to take chances with someone else's livelihood.
fieldNote: A **missed repair applicant** anchors her concern about exact-title searches despite fluent AI use.
Her **eight-month reserve** and partner's wage support household security without easing her fairness standard.

steps.text: Keep human review of shortlisted applicant work samples
Save 200 monthly per child in education accounts while both salaries hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our recruiters Steady Disruption will write job adverts, screen applications and book interviews faster, and we need to test who is excluded before accepting any speed target. I'd ask staff representatives to see the rejection reasons beside the tool's scores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A larger team could run with fewer recruiters and maybe fewer managers; I am capable, not exceptional, and the company could combine my team with another. My savings and a busy local hiring market give me options, but I don't want to be the person who taught a tool to ignore practical experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll run a six-week comparison on one maintenance job, with applicants' permission and staff representatives checking rejected work samples. In the first year of disruption, if the comparison passes, I'd configure the tool to flag missing experience rather than auto-reject; if my manager post goes, I'd seek another hiring team only where the vacancy is real and the pay keeps our mortgage and child care covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a team cut, even as I want the screening test done well. An applicant's missing interview is not a rounding error in my dashboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would fail the comparison?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tool rejects a qualified repair worker that the manual panel would interview, I'd stop automatic sorting for that vacancy. I would make the rejected sample visible to the staff representatives, without revealing the applicant's private details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lead the rollout if it reduces staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with the staffing plan and an appeal route open to recruiters and applicants. I won't tell my team a pilot is harmless when I can see the headcount sheet.

say: I'd seek a **six-week comparison** of rejected applicants before accepting faster screening targets.
I'd let **staff representatives** inspect reasons for rejection without exposing private candidate details.
think: My **manager role** could be merged if fewer recruiters handle a larger applicant pool.
Savings and local options help, but I fear helping a tool **miss practical skill**.
do: Compare **one maintenance vacancy** for six weeks with applicant consent and representative review.
Configure **experience flags** only if the test passes and staffing plus appeal terms are open.
If cut, seek **posted hiring work** only at pay covering mortgage and childcare.
feel: She feels **anxious** about a manager cut and a qualified applicant being excluded.
S1.quote: An applicant's missing interview is not a rounding error in my dashboard.
fieldNote: Her **maintenance work sample** gives a concrete fairness test beyond a generic claim about bias.
She would lead a rollout only after **staffing and appeal terms** are visible to her team.

steps.text: Give staff representatives rejected work samples from consented six-week test
Configure experience flags only if test passes and staffing plan plus appeal route are open
Apply for posted hiring manager roles if cut and pay covers mortgage and childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our team AGI by 2028 can screen and interview nearly any candidate as well as us, and the company owes both applicants and staff an appeal route before posts disappear. I'd ask for a dated staffing decision and a named person who can reopen a rejected application.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hiring work is thinking work in 2028; robots around 2031 do not postpone the risk. I could lose a well-paid post, but eight months saved, my partner's salary and many local employers let us search without missing the next mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll bring our missed repair candidate case to staff representatives and ask for written notice terms. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, I'd review its rejected applications against real work samples if I still have access; if my post goes, I'd apply for local talent development roles only where a posted vacancy has mortgage-covering pay, and keep working until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing the team and the salary, not overwhelmed. I would still feel sick if the system shut a skilled worker out before anyone could appeal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would talent development be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No; planning training and evaluating people are thinking work too. A development job would give us wages while I build other skills, not a promise of shelter from AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them our home and school are steady for now because we saved, but I may have to change jobs. I won't ask them to carry my worry as though a job application were already a redundancy letter.

say: I'd demand **staffing dates** and a named person to reopen wrong rejections.
I'd tell recruiters **screening changes in 2028**, before physical robots arrive.
think: My **hiring role** faces 2028 AGI; 2031 robots do not extend the deadline.
Eight months saved and local employers let us cover the **next mortgage** during a search.
do: Bring the **missed repair case** to representatives and request written notice terms now.
After 2028, review **AGI rejections** if employed; seek posted development work with mortgage pay if cut.
Accept only a **written offer** before leaving the current hiring team.
feel: She feels **anxious** about a possible cut and skilled applicants being shut out.
S2.quote: A development job would give us wages while I build other skills, not a promise of shelter from AGI.
fieldNote: She places **AGI screening in 2028** and admits that talent development is thinking-exposed too.
Her cushion supports a **measured search**, while her appeal demand includes applicants as well as staff.

steps.text: Ask staff representatives for written notice terms using missed repair candidate case
Review AGI rejected applications against work samples after 2028 if employed
Apply for posted talent development only if pay covers mortgage after cut
Accept a new role only after a written offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell recruiters AGI by 2031 gives us time to practice the hard candidate conversations and make sure rejection appeals are real. I'd ask the company to fund supervised interview practice, not just buy a newer screening system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let me move into apprenticeship support and help people show skills they learned outside school. But AI can match skills and plan apprenticeships in 2031 too; robots around 2034 may reach physical work later, not spare my management desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From next spring, if the company pays for the hours, I'd spend one afternoon a month with its apprenticeship coordinator and practise interviewing applicants who have no formal certificate. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd seek a posted apprenticeship lead job only if it pays enough for our mortgage and care costs; otherwise I'd look at local employers with real openings while staying on my present salary until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about changing the kind of hiring I know. Five years is enough to learn if the company gives actual people and paid time to work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look beyond certificates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The repair candidate we missed had done the work for years and lacked the exact title on the form. I want to ask what someone can do before I ask which word appears on their CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your company will not fund the afternoons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing work samples in my current role and ask staff representatives to request paid practice. I won't use family time for an unpaid placement that serves the company's future staffing plan.

say: I'd ask for **paid interview practice** and genuine rejection appeals before 2031.
I'd tell recruiters to seek **demonstrated skill** beyond the words on a certificate.
think: Five years might let me build **apprenticeship experience** with applicants outside formal routes.
Skill matching and training plans remain **thinking work** exposed in 2031; later robots add no delay.
do: Practise **monthly apprentice interviews** next spring only if company funds hours and coordinator guides me.
After 2031, seek **posted apprenticeship lead** only with mortgage-and-care pay.
If no lead role exists, seek **local openings** while keeping current salary until a signed offer.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about a new route but able to practise if the time is paid.
S3.quote: I want to ask what someone can do before I ask which word appears on their CV.
fieldNote: She uses a **real missed applicant** to target supervised interviewing rather than another screening course.
Apprenticeship planning stays **thinking-exposed** and any next role depends on pay and a posted vacancy.

steps.text: Practise monthly apprenticeship interviews if company pays and coordinator guides
Apply for posted apprenticeship lead after 2031 only if pay covers mortgage and childcare
Apply locally if no lead role exists, keeping salary until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff council AGI by 2036 gives us ten years to make applicant appeals ordinary, not a favor granted after a complaint. I'd ask for yearly figures on who was rejected, who appealed and who got a second look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 our children will be older, while a smaller mortgage is possible but not guaranteed. I could spend a decade helping people move between careers, but career advice is also thinking work AGI can do in 2036; robots around 2039 do not keep a desk manager safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep work-sample reviews and join the council's yearly audit of rejected applicants. I'll also take a self-funded evening mediation course for at most 800 from our training account, so I can handle an appeal meeting myself; in the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd stay only for a paid role with real authority to reconsider a rejection, otherwise seek local roles while keeping my job until a signed offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm enough to invest in a new skill, though I know the field can change. Ten years and our savings give me time to find out where my judgment actually helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your children's studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would tell them to keep learning what interests them and let us handle the mortgage; I won't turn a distant work scenario into their school timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a real appeal look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rejected applicant could show me a repair they completed, and I could put that evidence before a hiring panel that can change its mind. A polite email with no second look is not an appeal.

say: I'd seek **yearly appeal figures** and a real second look for rejected applicants.
I'd ask staff to make **appeals ordinary**, not dependent on a special favor.
think: At **53**, children will be older, while a smaller mortgage remains uncertain.
Career advice remains **thinking work** exposed in 2036; robots around 2039 offer no desk delay.
do: Keep **work-sample reviews** and join the council's yearly rejection audit.
Take a **self-funded mediation course** costing at most 800; stay after 2036 only with paid appeal authority.
Seek **local roles** otherwise, keeping current job until a signed offer arrives.
feel: She feels **calm enough** to invest in learning, while alert to change in her field.
S4.quote: A polite email with no second look is not an appeal.
fieldNote: Her long-run plan asks whether an **appeal panel can change** its decision, not simply send a reply.
A **strong reserve** enables self-funded mediation without claiming career advice is safe from AGI.

steps.text: Keep reviewing applicant work samples this year
Join yearly staff council audit of rejected applicants
Take self-funded mediation course costing at most 800
Seek local roles after 2036 if no paid appeal authority, keeping job until signed offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because hiring teams could shrink before candidates and recruiters have a working appeal route. A dated staffing plan, tested work-sample checks and real openings with pay we can live on would help me make a measured move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the repair worker whose title did not match our form whether a person ever looked at the work sample. A form can be complete while a person's chance is missing.

headlineQuote: A form can be complete while a person's chance is missing.
portrait: At **43**, Dana manages six recruiters and uses AI daily, while reading candidates' work samples herself.
Her **eight-month reserve**, high pay and many local teams support careful moves despite a mortgage and two children.
She tests **rejected applicants** with staff representatives and insists on a real second look.
Fast AGI threatens **hiring screens**; longer runways let her practise apprenticeship interviews, though that work remains exposed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink her hiring team before a useful applicant appeal is in place.
whatWouldHelp: A **staffing date**, tested work-sample checks and viable local roles would let her move carefully.
